Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: This avoidance item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For toxic chemical exposure, the reported triggers, threat beliefs, and memory problems center on unpredictability, loud sounds, incomprehensible chatter, and difficulty verbalising the event. Avoidance of military or police uniforms/weapons implies a different threat context involving armed authority or assault, and there are no corresponding trigger, threat, or memory items linking the trauma to uniforms, weapons, or law-enforcement cues. This creates a clinically implausible mismatch within the five components.

vignette:
Marianne, a 51-year-old European American civil servant, had been working for years in a municipal office where the routine of paperwork and public enquiries usually suited her. The event that changed that sense of order happened at a workplace storage facility, when a sealed container of toxic chemicals was opened unexpectedly and a sharp, choking odour spread through the room. People started speaking at once, voices overlapping in a way she could not make sense of, and although no one seemed to know exactly what was happening, she remembers the confusion more than any clear sequence. In the first days afterward, whenever someone talked about the incident or mentioned the facility, Marianne found herself going blank. She would start to explain what had happened and then lose the thread completely, as if the details were there but unreachable, and even when she tried deliberately to call the memory up, she could not get hold of it in words. What remained was fragmentary and nonverbal: the smell, the sense of danger, and the feeling that her body had understood something her mind could not yet say.

That inability to explain the event became part of what frightened her. Marianne noticed that when colleagues asked her what had happened, she would rehearse her answers in her head before speaking, and still the moment of telling often collapsed into hesitation or silence. Because the memory stayed so hard to access and so difficult to put into language, she began to avoid any situation that might expose that gap: she kept away from hospitals and ambulances, and even a routine physical examination made her tense, as if medical settings might force her back toward the thing she could not fully describe. At the same time, the event's uncanny qualities made ordinary unpredictability feel dangerous. A sudden change in plan, a noisy room, or incomprehensible chatter in a corridor could bring back the same sense of being thrown into confusion, and she would immediately feel on edge. She became especially watchful when people approached without warning, including strangers in ordinary places, because her body had come to expect that danger could arrive just as abruptly as it had that day. Unexpected or loud sounds kept her on high alert, and she described feeling safe only in a very limited number of places, usually her own home or a few familiar routes she had mapped out carefully.

Over time, Marianne's efforts to manage this fear began to shape the very situations that made it worse. She rehearsed conversations before nearly any interaction, from a brief exchange at work to a greeting at the door, trying to prevent herself from freezing or losing her words. But the more she relied on rehearsing, the more she noticed that any unscripted moment felt risky, and that heightened vigilance made her scan for danger in unfamiliar voices, approaching people, and sudden noises all the more intensely. Physical contact became another source of strain: she would pull back from a handshake, stiffen if someone brushed past her, and avoid being touched in almost any context, which left her feeling more separate and more exposed when she was out in public. Even in the civil service office, where she had once moved comfortably among colleagues and visitors, she now sat rigidly at her desk, dreading interruptions and trying to keep her world narrow enough to feel manageable. The very habits she used to protect herself were gradually feeding the sense that the world beyond those few safe places was unsafe, and the more she narrowed her life, the more threatening ordinary contact and everyday movement seemed.

By the time she sought help, Marianne was distressed by how tightly the fear, the fractured memory, and the avoidance had become linked. Talking about the incident was still enough to make the memory fragment, and the fragmenting memory in turn kept the event vivid and unfinished, as though it might break through at any moment in a smell, a sound, or a stranger's sudden approach. She was exhausted by the constant rehearsing, the vigilance around noise and people, and the way she kept herself protected by staying in only the places that felt familiar. What finally brought her to treatment was the realization that she was no longer simply avoiding the toxic exposure itself, but also shrinking away from the ordinary parts of life that reminded her of it. She hoped that therapy might help her make sense of what had happened and find a way to speak about it without losing the thread, though what she feared most was that any fuller reminder would once again leave her flooded by the same helpless sense of threat.
